item.title: From CV to Proof of Contributions (PoC): How Engineers Can Prove Their Skills and Impact
item.author: Verlaine j muhungu
item.content:encoded: Don’t Focus Too Much on Your Resume, Focus on Skills FirstThe world of work will never be the same anymore, with AI disrupting many fields and changing the way we learn. But what about recruiting engineers and developers?For many years, a CV was seen as a measure of intelligence, expertise, and credibility. But have you ever seen an engineer or developer who seems different from what is written on three or five pages?The world we live in today has changed a lot with AI. With quantum computing, many things will change. We are at the dawn of a new era in the history of humanity. Machines will perform better than humans in some areas, so we will be obliged to focus on critical tasks where AI is not shining yet.After observing how the world of work is changing, in my opinion, we don’t need a CV anymore to hire engineers and developers. We need something new called a (PoC), with a mindset of: “Show me what you have done, not what you tell me.”This is what we need as the world we live in changes at a pace we can’t imagine.The world of work in 2026 with AIIn 2026, work is about collaborating with AI and improving workflows rather than competing with it. The focus is no longer on memorizing facts; it’s more about guiding AI, collaborating with it, and validating its outputs.A CV is to corporate work what memorization is to traditional education. The present and future of work require skills that some people were not prepared for.With traditional education, we memorize facts, get scores, earn degrees, and then sometimes fail in life to adapt to an uncertain world. This is where traditional education is weak. What is education for?Yesterday, we used to talk only to teachers, mentors, and coaches. Now, we talk with machines when the people we care about the most are not available. Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini are becoming part of our learning and personal development.In 2026, we are still debating whether AI is good or whether it is mature enough, until we lose some roles!By observing the data from 2023, we are getting closer to a world where a CV will no longer be enough for employability.Workers should be called in this new modern economy. Your value will be measured more by what you build, learn, and share with the world.Nobody cares if you have a long CV. Your contributions matter, and the global job landscape is becoming increasingly competitive.Bye to the curriculum vitae : a proof of contributions should be the new passport for employabilityYour contributions matter, and the global job landscape is becoming more competitive.After observing how the corporate world works and the changes we are seeing in the world today, the idea of a came to my mind, with this claim:A CV tells you what someone claims to have done; a Proof of Contributions shows what they actually did.An engineer can claim : But a proof of contributions could show :Open source contributionsCertifications and learningMetrics and measurable impact. Ttalks, mentorship, or knowledge sharingThis is what a Proof of Contributions should look like**:**What did you build, solve, create, or contribute?What problem were you solving?Tools, languages, platforms, methodologiesGitHub repo, demo, article, documentation, presentation, deployment, etc.Quantifiable results of your contribution**Who did you work with and what was your responsibility?What did the contribution teach you?When and how long did you work on it?This article reflects my thinking and vision of the future world of work for developers and engineers. I believe a Proof of Contributions (PoC) should be considered as a new way of demonstrating skills and professional value.As you read this article, keep in mind that this is still experimental. There are more contributions coming to support this work and develop an idea that I have been thinking about for a while.A CV can describe your professional journey, but it cannot always demonstrate what you are capable of doing. A Proof of Contributions () takes a different approach by showing the projects you have worked on, the problems you have solved, the knowledge you have gained, and the value you have shared with others.As AI makes it easier to create polished resumes and describe skills convincingly, simply making claims about your abilities will become less meaningful. What matters more is having evidence behind those claims.“”I believe the way we think about employability needs to change. A CV can tell us where someone has worked and what they claim to know, but contributions give us a better picture of what someone is capable of doing.The projects you build, the problems you solve, the code you share, the articles you write, the knowledge you contribute, and the results you achieve can become evidence of your skills.This is why I believe a Proof of Contributions () deserves a place in the future of hiring developers and engineers.This is still an experiment and a work in progressDon’t just tell people what you can do. Show them what you have contributed.

item.title: 5 Principles to Make Your Tech Product Hard to Ignore and Easy to Trust
item.author: Daria Volkova
item.content:encoded: Most founders think their trust problem is that people don't believe them. Usually, users can’t even tell what the product does.Here's the page you've seen a hundred times: purple gradient, a wordmark that could belong to four thousand other companies, dots connected by lines, and a stock photo of a team that doesn't work there.The product works, the team may be good, but there is the same visual for you and a hundred of your competitors. A person on the other side of the screen might think it looks like AI slop, or you just haven’t clarified your positioning and own style.I work with tech founders on positioning, product marketing, and brand strategy, and most of that job comes down to making a product trustworthy for the right audience.AI-generated marketing and design flattened everything. AI products that read as hype. Privacy tools nobody understands. Fintech startups that can't say what they do.Here are five principles I use to fix it. They work anywhere you're asking people to trust something they don't fully understand.1. People don't trust what they don't understandThe most common trust failure in tech is confusion. Your visitor doesn't think you're lying. They just can't tell what you actually do.In blockchain and crypto, projects hid behind "permissionless meta-infrastructure" and "sybil-resistant quadratic staking." Phrases like that wall you off from everyone who isn't already an insider.The same is happening in AI now: "agentic workflows," "multi-modal reasoning," "RAG-optimized pipelines." The technical people nod. Everyone else closes the tab.The move is to translate complexity into something a human can hold.Stripe built the most respected documentation in fintech, clear enough to integrate payments in an afternoon, deep enough that a serious engineer trusts it completely.Documentation like that is trust infrastructure. If your audience can't explain your product to a friend, they won't recommend it, and word of mouth is the strongest distribution there is.2. Clarity beats clevernessThe buzzwords - disruptive, frictionless, cutting-edge, AI-native, meta infrastructure - are what you reach for when you haven't decided what you do.One test: say what you do, and the benefit it delivers, in a single sentence. If you can't, fix that before anything else. Wise built a brand on one line: send money abroad without the hidden fees, plus a tool that shows exactly how much your bank hides in the exchange rate. You get the value in five seconds.Now read your own landing page out loud. Most of them sound like a committee trying to impress a VC. They should sound like a person explaining something they care about.3. Branding makes you realPeople judge the design before they get to the words. Technical founders dismiss this constantly."We're a serious tech company, we don't need branding." Of course, you do! It's the fastest signal the brain processes.Think of Uniswap's pink unicorn, recognizable in a millisecond across every surface. Consistency reads as stability. It says this team has its act together.What reads as the “anti-trust“ signals:branding that changes between your site and your deck and your Twitterheavy 3D animation over a thin producta site that copies how the credible projects lookmimicking branding of legit projectsUsers can't name why your site feels sketchy. They feel it, and they leave. In AI, this is everywhere. The template I described at the top is running on 10 thousand sites right now, and every one of them inherits the reputation of the worst company using it.A distinctive, consistent identity says you'll still be here next year, and nobody trusts a company they expect to disappear.4. The gap between promise and reality is where trust diesBranding buys the first impression. It doesn't survive a gap between what you promised and what you shipped.Picture the juicy burger in the ad next to the sad one at the counter. That's what happens when marketing outpaces delivery: MVP in the press release versus the final product.The gap between promise and reality is where trust dies.In fintech, the gap opens on compliance. The product launches, then anti-money-laundering reviews and licensing turn the roadmap into a waiting room.In AI, it opens on accuracy. Benchmark ambitions in the launch post, hallucinated output in the user's first week.The answer is to make the work visible:Use your own product in public. If your team doesn't, no one else will either. Meet your users in person, at events, on calls.Ship regular public updates: visible progress and honest retrospectives when things break, not a polished quarterly post. The record is verifiable.The strongest signal isn't anything you say. It's whether real people talk about your work when you're not in the room.You've seen the account with 300, 000 followers, 5 likes per post, and bots in the comments. You know what it means: the audience is fake, so maybe the project is too. Follower count is the most gameable metric in tech, which is making it worthless as proof that anything is working. The ratio still talks, though.The market is learning to look at engagement quality, and whether real people are talking about your work unprompted.When your founders, engineers, and designers build their own reputations next to the product, that earns trust no paid promotion can match. In a low-trust market, your name is your product's first trust signal. I shared in one of my recent articles on Hackernoon.All five come down to the same instruction: make the true things about your company easy to see and hard to fake. Teach the category, say what you do in one line, look like you'll last, ship in the open, let other people carry your name.Trust takes months to build and one bad week to lose. A broken promise, a misleading demo, an inconsistent message, and the credibility is gone. It takes more patience than most founders want to spend. The ones who spend it are the ones people still trust when the market turns.💬 Have a story to share or want to add your advice for tech founders? Let me know in the comments.

item.title: Congratulations on Your Flawless AI Agent. Too Bad the Business Runs on Slack.
item.author: Muin Can Kisi
item.content:encoded: If you want to know why your shiny new enterprise AI tool has a 5% adoption rate, go look at the database schema the client handed you when you first starting prototyping for this project:It’s probably beautiful. Perfectly normalised. You spent ages cleaning foreign keys and making sure you have absolute zero redundancy. Your looked at that pristine data sample, and you felt the instant urge to hook up an LLM and build some sick RAG pipeline, you made sure the embeddings are as beautiful as the original data and your new baby is deployed as an agent that technically answers every question, specifically and exclusively from the client’s knowledge base.You go into the client demo buzzing with excitement. The executives and managers love it and love you! the demo makes total sense to them. So, you hit deploy. You push it to the live environment, expecting an even better feedback from the end users, the hands on employees. Instead, the real end-users take one look at it and go right back to their manual labour. Your day-one user count? Zero (0).Why? Because your schema reflects how management the company operated. But in reality, the actual business functions on undocumented employee operated workarounds.The reality of how a business operates doesn't live in a Postgres table or an Excel sheet. even if the client made it look like so, It lives in Slack DMs. private Google Doc cheat sheets, Zoom meeting transcripts. It lives in the gut feeling of a senior analyst who knows that "Pending" actually means "Approved but waiting on Finance, so go ahead and ship it anyway."If you build AI based purely on what's in the business knowledge base, you build based on the business outcome and not the workflow, If you want to build AI that people actually use from Day 1, you need to extract the juicy, undocumented subject matter expert (SME) knowledge that actually lead eventually into the business outcome.And how to catch that fish in this enormous lake of knowledge? You send a fisherman, a Forward Deployed Engineer.The Limit of the SpreadsheetStandard software development is basically a long chain of Zoom calls. The client tells an account manager their problem, who tells a product manager, who writes a spec, who hands it to an engineer who has never met the end-user, never heard of the client company before, and don’t even care to know.When building traditional solutions, you can somewhat get away with this (from personal experience). But AI is different. AI is supposed to mimic human reasoning, feel natural, and be your buddy who knows all your cheeky little shortcuts.When an engineer tries to build an AI agent using only historical data and spreadsheets, the agent lacks . It doesn't know a decision was made, only that it made, with zero context of the many wrong undocumented decisions made before finding the right path.A CRM record states that a $100k enterprise deal was closed at 11:58 PM on the last day of the quarter. Your model checks the timestamp and concludes that midnight is the perfect time to send contract proposals. It doesn't know the deal was actually sealed three weeks earlier over drinks, and the sales rep is always late, and they were logging it in the parking lot to hit their quota before the system locked them out.If you don't capture that of problem-solving, your AI will just confidently generate naive textbook solutions that make industry experts give each other a funny look.Deploy the Engineer, Not Just the CodeA Forward Deployed Engineer isn't just a consultant in a suit, and they aren't your typical backend developer. They are software engineers who live in the trenches with the client, gifted with a sixth sense for spotting exactly where automation will create massive value.They sit on the trading floor. They shadow the logistics dispatchers. They watch the procurement officers scream at their monitors.Their entire job is to bridge the massive gap between and .When an FDE sits next to an SME, they aren't just looking at the output; they are mapping the expert’s internal logic. They ask the questions that never make it into a spec document:"Why did you ignore the dashboard and check that legacy portal instead?""What made you instantly reject that application without even scrolling down?""Why do you always format the payload this specific way on Fridays?"An FDE takes that juicy, unspoken SME knowledge and bakes it directly into the AI's prompts, tool-calling logic, and guardrails. Suddenly, the AI isn't just regurgitating database rows—it's thinking like the team's best operator.The Psychology of Day 1 AdoptionThere is a dirty secret in enterprise software: the hardest part of building AI isn't the technology, it's the change management.If you drop a fully baked AI tool onto an operations team from out of nowhere, they will reject it. They will view it as a threat, a nuisance, or an out-of-touch toy built by Silicon Valley tourists.This is where the FDE model creates absolute magic: When an FDE builds an AI agent the end-users—sitting next to them, tweaking the prompts in real-time based on their feedback, breaking the tool and fixing it together—a psychological shift happens.The end-users no longer feel like software is happening them. They feel like they are part of the development cycle. They aren't just users; they are co-creators."Hey, I told the engineer that the bot wasn't checking the compliance tags properly, and he pushed a fix 10 minutes later. Look, it's doing it my way now!"When launch day comes, you don't need a massive change-management seminar or mandatory training videos. The adoption is natural from Day 1 because the tool was molded around the operators' exact quirks, frustrations, and workflows.Data without context is just trivia.If you want to build AI that actually transforms a business, you have to stop building it in a vacuum. You have to put your engineers on the front lines, let them absorb the messy reality of the SME's daily grind, and translate that human intuition into agentic workflows.Because the best AI doesn't just read the client's database. It reads the room.

item.title: A Private Debt Crisis
item.author: Chris Gale
item.content:encoded: Leveraged buyouts were once a precision tool, effective when used selectively and with discipline. Today, leverage has become a default setting.Not to over indulge in contrastive negatives, but debt isn’t just part of the strategy, in many cases, it the strategy. If more investors get experience not using leverage, the cloak of normalization can be lifted before it’s too late. Wait too long, the wake up may be harsh.Where are troubles emerging? While not the same as leverage for buyouts, the way private credit has moved from the margins to the center of dealmaking is connected. By most industry accounts and publicly available data, private credit now funds a significant share of leveraged buyouts, particularly in the middle market. What was once an alternative to banks has become a core source of financing for sponsor‑led transactions.I’m not a private credit specialist (though I can introduce you to my nephew who is), and I won’t pretend to be one. We do, however, do a lot of work across industries, and with differing investment management firm strategies. So this is what we’ve seen. And I’d argue you don’t need to model loan structures to notice the broader implications. When the same ecosystem increasingly supplies both equity and debt, risk becomes more concentrated, even if it’s not immediately visible.That arrangement can work for a long time. Until it doesn’t.If critics are right and today’s private credit boom eventually runs into stress, the answer won’t come from inventing new structures that try to make expensive capital feel cheap again. It will come from rediscovering something far more durable, value creation that doesn’t rely on leverage doing most of the work.And this isn’t an argument against leverage itself. Used thoughtfully, leverage lowers the cost of capital, enables acquisitions, and can accelerate growth. But the industry has drifted to a point where leverage often functions less as a tool and more as an assumption. And when assumptions change—as they inevitably do, systems built on them are tested.Private equity investors are beginning to confront an uncomfortable question, how much of the past decade’s performance reflected genuine operational improvement, and how much was driven by financial structures made possible by years of abundant, inexpensive capital?As interest rates have reset, that question has become harder to avoid. Dealmakers and lenders alike have noted tighter interest coverage, more challenging refinancings, and less flexibility in capital structures that once appeared resilient. Returns that felt routine in a low‑rate environment are proving harder to reproduce.A capital‑allocation storyDebt‑heavy private capital didn’t emerge in isolation. It evolved alongside incentives that emphasized scale, speed, and near‑term outcomes. When leverage amplified success, it looked like innovation. When it amplifies vulnerability, it reveals how dependent many outcomes were on structure rather than substance.That’s why private capital without leverage can seem unconventional today, even though it’s not new.Buying and holding companies with little or no debt forces investors to return to fundamentals, customers, cash flow, and long‑term growth. Without leverage doing the heavy lifting, performance has to come from the business itself. Financial engineering can’t substitute for execution.In an unlevered model, returns are driven largely by profits. The pressure to mark assets up aggressively or rush toward exits diminishes. Companies are sold when it makes strategic sense, not because covenants, refinancing calendars, or fund timelines demand it. Investors can afford patience because cash isn’t diverted to servicing debt.Sales still happen. But they happen for reasons rooted in the business, when scale, complexity, or market position suggests a different owner, not because leverage forces the decision.It’s often said that debt enforces discipline. There’s truth in that. Lenders impose scrutiny, and underwriting can provide an external check. But discipline doesn’t have to come exclusively from leverage. It can come from alignment between investors and operators.Unlevered investors have to be explicit about how value will be created. When that exercise is taken seriously, it becomes clear that some deals are not just compatible with an unlevered approach, they’re better suited to it. Those opportunities often sit outside the traditional leveraged buyout mold.Small and medium‑sized businesses are a good example. By government and industry estimates, they make up nearly all U.S. companies, employ roughly half the private sector workforce, and account for a substantial share of economic output. Many are founder or family‑owned, profitable, and deeply connected to their communities. Maybe the margins are thin, but they’re also constant and so thin, that others don’t see a point in crowding in.Traditional leveraged buyout models frequently struggle to accommodate them. Growth takes time. Owners don’t want their legacy dismantled or their culture traded for short‑term margin expansion. Many want to remain involved, keep building, and preserve what they’ve created.Are they looking for an exit strategy? Not quite. What they’re looking for is a partner.That’s where patient, unlevered private capital can be most effective. When founders and families retain meaningful ownership and the balance sheet isn’t burdened by debt, incentives align quickly. The focus shifts from managing leverage to strengthening operations, investing in people, systems, and products that support sustainable growth.Risk doesn’t disappear. That’s investing. But it’s a different kind of risk, transparent, operational, and tied to real economic outcomes rather than interest‑rate paths or refinancing assumptions.The payoff looks different too. Instead of returns dominated by multiple expansion and leverage, gains come from businesses that generate durable earnings and are genuinely stronger when capital eventually rotates.As markets adapt to a higher cost of capital, investors face a choice. They can keep searching for ways to recreate the conditions of the past decade, new instruments, new structures, and new forms of leverage. Or they can step back and ask a simpler question, are returns coming from the business, or from the balance sheet?The private credit boom may not end in crisis. But it should mark a moment of reflection. The next chapter of private capital doesn’t need to reject leverage entirely, it just needs to stop relying on it as the primary engine of returns.That idea shouldn’t sound radical.The most resilient returns have always come from building better businesses, not from borrowing more against them.

item.title: Why Imperial Historians Want You to Forget Kharkiv’s Real Story [Breaking the Myths]
item.author: Arthur
item.content:encoded: If you listen to Russian state historians or read old Soviet textbooks, you’d think Kharkiv was popped out of thin air in 1925 by a panel of Bolshevik bureaucrats armed with concrete, steel, and a copy of .The narrative is always the same: “It’s an industrial city! It’s Russian-speaking! It’s basically Soviet property!”It’s a classic imperial playbook strategy: erase a city’s history, strip away its cultural context, rebrand it as a factory town, and then claim it as your own because people there happen to speak your language.But here’s the thing—calling Kharkiv a "Soviet creation" is like looking at a 300-year-old oak tree, noticing someone nailed a poster to it in 1950, and claiming the poster grew the tree. Let’s dismantle this garbage narrative piece by piece.1. The Freedom-Loving Outlaws Who Actually Founded the CityLong before Soviet planners built massive concrete blocks, Kharkiv was founded in the 1650s by Ukrainian Cossacks.These weren’t obedient subjects looking to serve a king or a tsar. They were —rebels, frontiersmen, and refugees fleeing Polish nobility and Muscovite overreach from Central and Western Ukraine. They settled in a region that came to be known as (Sloboda Ukraine).Notice the root word: Sloboda. It means freedom(not a correct translation, but i’ll keep it as it is my article).Settlers were granted "slobodas"—tax-free, autonomous settlements—in exchange for defending the frontier. The legendary Cossack Kharko (from whom the city gets its name, according to local tradition) didn’t build a fortress to serve Moscow. He and thousands of Ukrainian settlers built a fortress at the confluence of the Kharkiv and Lopan rivers because they wanted a place to live, trade, and fight on their own terms.By the 1660s, Kharkiv wasn't just an outpost; it was the regimental center of the Kharkiv Cossack Regiment. The legendary Zaporozhian Ottoman Ivan Sirko—the guy famous for sending a brutally sarcastic letter to the Ottoman Sultan—was literally a colonel of the Kharkiv Regiment. Sarcasm, autonomy, and refusing to bend to autocratic rulers are literally in the soil here.2. The Cultural Powerhouse Imperialists Try to IgnoreImperial historians love to claim that Ukrainian culture was just a "rural dialect" until the Soviets supposedly educated the masses. That is historically illiterate.The Birth of Modern Ukrainian Literature: Long before the Soviet Union existed, Kharkiv was the intellectual beating heart of Ukraine. In 1805, the University of Kharkiv was founded—not by the Tsar’s generosity, but largely funded by local Ukrainian gentry and Cossack descendants.The Romantic Movement: In the 1830s, the "Kharkiv Romantic School" laid the groundwork for modern Ukrainian national identity, publishing books, collecting folklore, and proving that Ukrainian was a rich, literary language while imperial censors were actively trying to ban it.The "Executed Renaissance": In the 1920s, Kharkiv became the stage for a massive explosion of avant-garde Ukrainian culture. Writers like Mykola Khvylovy, theater directors like Les Kurbas, and poets like Pavlo Tychyna lived in the famous (a building shaped like the letter "C" for , meaning "Word"). They produced world-class art that was fiercely Ukrainian.What did the Soviets do with this cultural renaissance?They shot them. Literally.By the 1930s, Stalin purged, executed, or exiled almost the entire generation of Kharkiv’s creators because their vision of Ukraine was too free, too European, and too independent. Rebranding Kharkiv as a "purely Soviet industrial city" was the final step in covering up that crime.3. The Language Trap: Speaking Russian Doesn't Make You Imperial PropertyOne of the most persistent arguments used by Russian propaganda today is language. The logic goes: "They speak Russian, therefore they want to be part of Russia."This ignores basic history. The dominance of the Russian language in Kharkiv wasn't a natural preference; it was the result of centuries of state-enforced Russification. From the (1863) and (1876)—which literally made publishing books or performing plays in Ukrainian illegal—to Soviet forced migrations and educational policies, the imperial state worked overtime to wipe out the language of the surrounding region.Yet, if you stepped just ten miles outside of Kharkiv’s city center into the surrounding villages, the population remained overwhelmingly Ukrainian-speaking for centuries. The city was an island of enforced imperial administration surrounded by an ocean of Ukrainian culture.More importantly, language does not equal loyalty. Assuming a Russian-speaking Ukrainian in Kharkiv wants imperial rule is like assuming an English-speaking Irishman wants to be ruled by the British Crown. It’s a complete misunderstanding of identity.4. The Industrialization MythDid the Soviets build massive factories in Kharkiv? Yes. The Kharkiv Tractor Plant (HTZ) and the massive Gosprom building are iconic pieces of 20th-century architecture.But industrialization wasn't a gift bestowed upon Kharkiv by Moscow out of the goodness of their hearts. Kharkiv was chosen as an industrial hub it was already a massive, wealthy, highly educated regional crossroads with deep trade roots established during the Cossack and Imperial eras.The Soviets built on top of a foundation that Ukrainian merchants, engineers, and workers had already spent centuries laying down.It is not the end of the story, but did I convince you?Kharkiv is not a "Soviet city," and it certainly isn't a "Russian city."It is a frontier fortress built by free-thinking Cossacks, an intellectual capital that preserved Ukrainian identity against imperial bans, and a resilient metropolis that has survived Tsars, Bolshevik purges, Nazi occupation, and modern bombardment.Here is an old ad for the cinema in the city center. I was in the modern verion of that cinema at 2018.The next time someone tries to sell you the myth that Kharkiv’s history started in 1917, remind them: the city was founded on the concept of —and it has been fighting to keep that freedom for nearly four centuries.5. From Tsarist Concrete to Street Canvas: The Architectural EvolutionImperial and Soviet regimes loved building imposing, sterile monoliths to make human beings feel small. But Kharkiv’s modern identity took those concrete walls and flipped them on their head.In recent decades, the city became an epicenter for avant-garde urban art—most notably through the work of .Hamlet didn't just paint murals; he completely reshaped how people interact with Kharkiv’s historic streets. His signature black-and-white street art, paired with philosophical, raw, and often deeply sarcastic Ukrainian text, turned decaying walls, archways, and bombed-out plywood shutters into an open-air museum. He stripped away the gray Soviet monotony and injected a distinct, hyper-modern soul straight into the city’s architectural arteries.Images from my personal archiveAlongside street artists, a new generation of visionary Ukrainian architects stepped up to defend and guide the city's built environment. Rather than letting developers steamroll historical heritage or rebuild in bland neo-imperial styles, these local architects fought to preserve original 19th-century facade details while integrating bold, modern European design.They treated Kharkiv’s historical spaces not as Soviet relics to be hidden, but as a living canvas that reflects resilience, innovation, and creative freedom.6. The Engineering DNA: Why Kharkiv Became Ukraine’s Silicon ValleyIf you worked in global tech anytime over the last two decades, odds are high that some of the backend code, QA frameworks, or cloud architecture you rely on was built by an engineer sitting in a coffee shop in Kharkiv.Propagandists like to pretend that Kharkiv’s technical prowess was a top-down gift from Soviet planners.The Soviets built factories, but the people built the brainpower.Kharkiv naturally evolved into Ukraine’s primary educational powerhouse. Institutions like the Kharkiv National University of Radio Electronics (NURE), the National Aerospace University (KhAI), and NTU "KhPI" created a massive density of world-class technical talent. We aren't talking about low-level script kiddies; we are talking about hard-math theoreticians, aerospace engineers, cyber-security specialists, and system architects.When the global digital revolution hit, Kharkiv didn't have to import talent—it had an endless assembly line of brilliant, cynical, hyper-logical young minds ready to disrupt the market:: Long before "remote work" was a corporate buzzword, Kharkiv’s software engineers and QA testers were quietly powering global enterprise platforms, startups, and fortune 500 tech stacks.: The city didn't just host IT companies; it built an organic, vibrant tech culture complete with massive developer hubs, tech clusters, and hacker spaces. It became a magnet for developers from all over the country.: What made Kharkiv tech professionals different wasn't just their ability to write clean code—it was their raw problem-solving mindset forged in a city that historically never had anything handed to it on a silver platter.Before the full-scale invasion tried to flatten its infrastructure, Kharkiv’s tech industry was literally soaring "up to the sky." And even under fire, that engineering foundation didn't disappear—it adapted, built defense tech, and proved once again that you can attack physical buildings, but you can’t bomb an entire city’s collective intellect.Kharkiv isn't a museum piece, a leftover Soviet factory site, or an imperial frontier waiting to be "reclaimed."It is a city forged by Cossacks who hated tyranny, preserved by intellectuals who refused to let their language die, painted by street artists who refuse to live in the gray, and coded by badass engineers who build the future while the past tries to drag them down.If anyone tries to tell you otherwise—hand them a history book, show them a Hamlet mural, and tell them to check the source code.

item.title: You Can’t Git Clone a Relationship: Build a Trust Stack
item.author: Vik Bogdanov
item.content:encoded: Pendulum’s Magnolia Sevenler has spent her career designing rooms—from festival crowds to founder dinners. Her case to technical founders who’d rather ship than schmooze is simple: trust is infrastructure, and most teams under-provision it.Most technical founders don't dislike people. They’ve simply had enough of bad networking.You know the kind: rooms where everyone is pitching, nobody is listening, and the most popular question is immediately followed by a glance over your shoulder. So they stay home, ship another feature, and tell themselves the product will speak for itself.That can work for a while. Then the company needs a lead investor, a senior engineer, a distribution partner, or advice from someone who has already survived the problem now blocking the roadmap. At that point, the missing relationship becomes visible, but it is usually too late to create it on demand.You can spin up another server in minutes. You can't git clone a relationship.That idea sits at the center of my conversation with , founder and CEO of Pendulum — the company behind the Founders Series, its invite-only program of curated founder-and-investor gatherings, alongside larger cultural events. Before applying that experience to startup communities, Sevenler worked around , , and the music festival.Her message to founders is not "network more." It is more practical: treat trust as part of the infrastructure your company will eventually depend on."We focus on high-growth sectors — Web3, AI, cybersecurity, robotics, and next-generation consumer innovation — because that's where the next category-defining companies are emerging," she told me. "There’s so much happening within tech right now, but the ecosystem is still incredibly fragmented. For us, it’s not just about fundraising or making a connection that pays off immediately. It’s about creating a place where someone might meet another founder who has already solved the problem they’re facing, an investor who knows the right person, or have a conversation that becomes meaningful six months down the line.“But what we're really curating for is mindset. We want founders who are bold, visionary, and building for scale, and investors who are willing to take early, informed bets on those teams."That matters more now than it did before. According to , in Q1 2026, global venture funding hit a record $297 billion. With 81% going to AI, roughly $188 billion of it (65% of the entire quarter) went to just four companies: OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and Waymo. For everyone outside that handful, capital still exists but access to it is narrowing fast.That makes the right introduction less of a soft skill and more of a core competency.Think of networking as infrastructureSo I put the objection to her directly: the engineer who eyes a curated founder dinner and thinks that's not for people like me, and wants to know what it actually costs to opt out. Her response reframes the role these relationships play in building a company:"It's tough to convince engineers to go to a social outing, but I'd tell them not to think of it as networking at all. Think of it as . You can build an incredible product, but companies don't grow in isolation. At some point you need capital, talent, distribution, partnerships, advice — and all of those things ultimately come through people."That's the mental-model shift, and it's the one HackerNoon readers are best equipped to grasp. You already spend on infrastructure you can't see the ROI of on day one — observability, CI, a second availability zone. You provision it because you know the failure mode of having it is catastrophic and arrives without warning.Relationships are the same class of investment: a trust stack sitting alongside your tech stack, provisioned quietly, long before the day it has to bear load.Don't force the build to prodPendulum has hosted plenty of founders who later found investors, co-founders, and career-altering relationships through its rooms. But Sevenler almost always hears those stories later — and that lag is the point.The founder who treats the evening as a transaction — one target, acquired before last call — is usually the one who leaves empty-handed."It's like dating — you meet, you have a conversation, you see if there's chemistry or alignment, and then the relationship develops from there," she said. "You can usually feel when someone walks into a room thinking, 'I need to meet an investor tonight,' versus genuinely wanting to meet interesting people and build relationships."An introduction isn't an investment; it's the start of a sequence: conversation, follow-up, evidence, alignment, decision. Trying to compress that into one evening is the human equivalent of shoving an untested build straight to production and hoping it holds.Magnolia’s advice: come with intention, not an agenda. Know why you're there and who you'd like to meet, then leave room for the connection you didn't plan, which, she says, is usually the valuable one.The standard critique of events like Pendulum's is that they reinforce existing networks instead of opening them — the same connected people, recycled. Sevenler agrees that's the failure mode, and says it's exactly what she's built against."If you only invite people who are already in the Rolodex, you end up with the same room over and over again, and that's not particularly interesting," she said. Pendulum finds people through referrals, active research, and its broader community, and it leans hard on a mechanic that technical founders will recognize as organic network growth: it asks founders to bring other founders as guests."The goal isn't to reward people for already being connected. It's to create the kind of room where someone who have the Rolodex can start building one."That's the whole point for the readers on the wrong side of the $297B wall. The value of a network isn't confirming the connections you have. It's manufacturing the ones you don't.The economics of saying noMagnolia says that most events monetize attendance. The math is simple, and it quietly lowers the bar: every empty chair is money left on the table, so the guest list swells until the room stops meaning anything.Pendulum's Founders Series inverts it."We work with partners who pay us to curate the room and create the experience, rather than relying on ticket sales to break even," Sevenler said. "We're not incentivized to fill seats; we're incentivized to make sure the right people are in the room."It's a subtle but important structural choice. By moving the revenue off the attendee and onto partners who value the curation itself, she removes the incentive that degrades almost every networking event on earth.The business model the quality control.Which raises the obvious question: how do you actually decide who's in?Screening for mindset, not résumésPendulum doesn't screen primarily on title or sector. It screens on mindset — a word that sounds fuzzy until Sevenler makes it concrete."We're looking for people who are curious, ambitious, open, and genuinely interested in other people," she said. "We pay attention to what someone is building, but also who they are, what they're interested in, who they surround themselves with, and whether they're someone who adds value to the community."A lot of that screening, she admits, is instinctive — pattern-matching earned over years of reading rooms. And the goal is deliberately not what you'd expect from an "elite" event."The goal isn't to create a room full of impressive résumés. It's to create an environment where the people are impressive ."This is also her answer to the line between curation and gatekeeping, which she draws sharply: "Curation is about creating a point of view and bringing together people who genuinely add something to the room. Gatekeeping is when exclusivity becomes the experience itself." One is a design decision. The other is a velvet rope for its own sake.And if you're wondering whether great production can substitute for great people — whether a stunning venue can carry a dead room — she's blunt:"You can always make a beautiful room, but you can't design chemistry."The festival-producer's edgeYou can't design chemistry, but you can learn to engineer the conditions for it, and that's what Sevenler spent years doing before Pendulum. Those cultural productions — F1 paddocks, Chainsmokers-and-Tiësto-scale festival crowds — sound like the opposite of startup life. She says they were closer to a rehearsal for it."We built the entire Worlds Away festival from scratch, so in a lot of ways it felt very similar to starting a new business," she told me. "I was used to creating experiences for 200–300 guests, so the biggest shift was taking everything I already knew and scaling it to a much larger level."The transferable skill wasn't logistics. It was learning what makes a room — which turns out to be exactly what most founder networking gets wrong.You can talk to 500 people and still build an intimate roomSevenler has a line that sounds like a paradox until you sit with it: intimacy is scalable. Most people assume the opposite — that closeness comes from keeping numbers small. She thinks that's precisely the trap."The biggest mistake is assuming that intimacy comes from having fewer people. It actually comes from having the people," she said. "You can have 500 people in a room and still create a very intimate experience if the community has a real point of view and people feel connected to why they're there. That is what makes a room work."For a technical audience, this is a familiar shape: the bottleneck isn't the number of nodes in the graph; it's the quality of the edges. A room of 500 with dense, high-trust connections beats a room of 50 who have no reason to talk to each other.So where does it break? Not at a headcount — at a motive."Dilution happens when growth starts dictating the guest list rather than the other way around," she explained. "A new city or partner should give us access to a new pocket of people, culture, or energy that makes the events more interesting. If we're adding something just to make the footprint bigger, that's when I think you lose the magic."That's a discipline most growth-obsessed companies never develop: refusing scale that doesn't improve the product.It's the events equivalent of resisting feature creep — every new city, partner, or sponsor looks attractive on its own and still degrades the system as a whole. Pendulum keeps New York and LA as anchors and runs destination events where its community already converges — Miami, Vegas, Austin, London — rather than planting a flag in every city. "We don't want Pendulum to feel like an event that happens everywhere. We want each experience to feel like something that could only happen in that city, with those people, at that moment."Luxury is the interface, not the functionThere's an obvious failure mode for events built around F1 paddocks and Fashion Week: the production becomes the point. A stunning venue photographs well, performs on social media, and can make a room valuable before a single useful conversation happens. Substance quietly gets replaced by set dressing."Luxury becomes a problem when it becomes the reason for the room," she said. "For us, the F1 paddock, Fashion Week, or an incredible venue is the — not the substance."Used correctly, though, culture does real work. It gives strangers a shared thing to react to and strips out the formality that makes traditional networking so joyless. "You're not walking into a ballroom with a name tag and being told to network," she said. "You're experiencing something together, and the conversation happens much more naturally around it." The venue is the UI; the connections are the function underneath – and no amount of front-end polish fixes an empty one.The room is a product: build a minimum viable oneHere's the reframe that should click for anyone who ships software: the room is a product. It has users (the guests), a spec (the reason they're all there), and a failure mode (a dead room nobody wants to come back to). Everything Sevenler does — the screening, the pricing, the refusal to scale for scale's sake — is product design applied to a guest list. And the best part is that you don't need a Pendulum invite to ship your own version. Its smallest viable release needs no famous venue and no global guest list.When I asked what one thing a founder reading this could take from how she builds rooms, her answer wasn't "apply and wait." It was "build your own version" — and the instructions are almost aggressively simple:"Invite five people you genuinely find interesting to dinner, and ask each of them to bring one person you don't know. You've just built a room of ten people with a reason to trust each other, and potentially started your own network."That's your minimum viable room.Five people you vouch for, each bringing one node you can't reach — trusted introductions, zero cold outreach, a built-in reason for strangers to extend each other credit. It's the referral mechanic that grows Pendulum, compressed to a dinner table and a budget of one reservation. Ship it, notice which conversations had energy, and invite again. The next version tunes itself around a specific problem, market, or stage of the company — and a few iterations in, you've built the one piece of infrastructure you can't spin up on demand.With two-thirds of venture funding flowing to just four companies, building the right relationships may be one of the smartest investments available to everyone else. As Sevenler puts it, you don’t need to know everyone. You need to know the right few.The product still matters. It always will. But companies do not scale on code alone. Capital, talent, distribution, advice, and unexpected opportunities all move through people. Building trust is not a distraction from the work; it is part of the stack, and the best time to provision it is before you need it.If your startup needed a relationship tomorrow that you couldn’t build overnight, would your trust stack be ready?

item.title: The Fake Executive Funnel: When Job Offers Become Free Labor
item.author: Lomit Patel
item.content:encoded: During a recent interview process for a senior marketing/growth executive role, the company pivoted mid-process from a salaried offer to an unpaid, revenue-share advisory agreement instead. I didn't sign it. This piece breaks down how that funnel works, why the contract mechanics make it a bad trade, and what operators and founders should do about it. I've generalized identifying details so this can't be traced back to the company involved.When early-stage AI startups hit a capital constraints wall, standard Lean operating discipline says tighten feedback loops, focus on high-retention cohorts, and use automation to lower Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC).I recently sat through an interview process for a senior marketing/growth executive role. It started straightforward, then partway through, the terms changed. I'm not naming the company, and since then I've heard other operators describe versions of the same thing happening to them. What matters here isn't who did it to me. It's how the mechanics work, because it isn't isolated.This sits next to a trend that's already drawing regulatory attention. State lawmakers have begun targeting "ghost job" postings, listings companies post with no real intent to fill, and the Congressional Research Service has published a brief on the practice. What I'm describing here is a more calculated variant: not a listing that goes nowhere, but a real interview process that quietly converts into free labor once the company has what it needs.The role was posted as salaried, with real cross-functional ownership, competitive compensation, and equity on the table. After a couple of interviews, that changed. It went something like this (paraphrased, not word for word):We love your background, but our board recommended pausing the full-time role until our next raise. In the meantime, we'd love to bring you on as an Advisor on our Advisory Board.Instead of an executive contract, a retainer, or a standard FAST equity grant, what showed up was an asymmetric agreement offering a revenue share, in the 30% to 50% range, on any clients or demand partners I introduced.I don't think this was a one-off hiring delay. Structured the way it was, it reads like a systematic, near-zero-cost customer acquisition shortcut, dressed up as executive recruitment. I didn't sign it. Here's why.The Fake Executive Funnel1. EXECUTIVE BAIT Salaried marketing/growth executive job posting │ ▼ 2. STRATEGY EXTRACTION Candidate reveals ICPs, GTM playbooks, and account lists │ ▼ 3. THE RECRUITMENT PIVOT "Role on hold. Join our Advisory Board instead." │ ▼ 4. UNPAID CAC EXTRACTION 100% revenue-share / affiliate contract • $0 base, $0 equity, $0 retainer • Unilateral lead-exclusion window • Payment lags of 90+ days The Psychological ConversionThe pivot from "executive offer" to "commission-only contract" doesn't happen on contract terms alone. In my case, three things stood out, and in hindsight they were doing specific work to move me from expecting a C-suite offer to signing a lead-gen agreement: Language that flattered by suggesting I'd be part of a small, exclusive group shaping the category. I was being led to feel selected, not redirected. Any hesitation, or the ordinary due diligence of actually reading the agreement, got framed as the real risk, more than the terms themselves. The pressure was to sign quickly, not to look closely. An official company email address costs a company nothing, but it creates the feeling of being an insider, even as the contract explicitly disclaimed any employment, worker, or agency relationship.What It Does to Unit EconomicsIn , I write about how high-performing startups use machine learning, automated experimentation, and data integrations to scale acquisition with lean teams. The goal of modern GTM architecture is a repeatable system where $1 of input predictably returns more than $3 of Lifetime Value (LTV) within a defined payback window.This pattern is the inverse of that. It's an operational shortcut that masks broken unit economics rather than fixing them, in three ways:Artificial CAC suppression. Shifting the work of door-opening, lead qualification, and social selling onto unpaid executive candidates makes CAC look near $0 on paper, because the labor behind it is uncompensated. During a multi-round interview loop, candidates walk through GTM teardowns, ideal customer profiles, and channel strategy on the assumption they're competing for a real role. The company collects senior growth architecture for free. When a seasoned operator lists "Advisor at [Company]" on LinkedIn, the company borrows that operator's credibility to signal maturity to investors and enterprise buyers it hasn't yet earned.Inside the RevShare ContractContracts like this tend to share a few mechanisms. Here's what stood out in mine, generalized to the pattern rather than the specifics of one document:Standard Executive AdvisoryThe "Fake CMO" RevShare ContractFAST equity (0.25%–1.0%) or a monthly cash retainer$0 base, $0 retainer, $0 equityOpen CRM access, mutual attributionCompany has sole discretion to accept or reject a leadMonthly retainer or standard Net 30Quarterly in arrears, Net 90 (often 6–7 months out)Ongoing alignment with LTVCapped at 6 months post go-liveThree terms are what made me stop:The discretionary lead exclusion. Agreements like this commonly give the company a window (often around 10 business days) to accept or reject an introduced lead, sometimes with the right to decline if the prospect is already "in our CRM," a claim the candidate has no way to verify. Without audit rights into the company's pipeline, the company can simply decline the referral, wait out the contract, and close the relationship directly later with no commission owed. Commissions are frequently calculated on net revenue actually collected, tallied quarterly in arrears, and paid 90 days after quarter close. As an example: an operator who opens an enterprise door in January, with the quarter closing March 31, wouldn't see cash until late July. That's a seven-month window where the operator carries all of the front-end risk. Enterprise account ramps are rarely linear. Integration and testing can run 3 to 6 months before volume scales. Capping commission eligibility at 6 months from go-live means the operator does the hard work of opening the door while the company keeps the long-term value.The B2B Attribution ProblemBeyond the hiring ethics, this exposes a real flaw in how early-stage teams think about B2B attribution. Consumer affiliate mechanics (click, then buy) don't map onto complex enterprise sales.Enterprise deals move through executive introductions, committee review, security and legal diligence, and procurement, often looping back through direct or organic touchpoints before signature. When a startup tries to measure door-opening with consumer-style affiliate attribution, the person who spent years building the trust that got the meeting is usually the first one stripped out of the model as the deal moves downstream.The Real Cost: Spent Social CapitalEvery senior operator spends years building personal distribution authority. Introducing an unproven, early-stage platform to that network converts hard-won trust into commercial velocity on the company's behalf.If the product underperforms, fails a security review, or mishandles delivery, the company loses a customer. The operator loses something harder to replace: professional trust. Trading that for a non-guaranteed, heavily capped commission is a bad exchange. That's ultimately why I passed.If you're a senior operator or executive candidate:Name the pivot when it happens. If a hiring conversation shifts from a salaried role to an unpaid advisory or commission-only arrangement, stop and ask directly: "What's the guaranteed base compensation or standard equity structure for this scope of work?"Protect your account data. Show strategic capability through frameworks and cohort-level results, not by handing over specific target account lists or warm leads in an interview. If you do agree to advise an early-stage company, ask for a standard Founder Institute FAST Agreement: roughly 0.25% to 1.0% equity, vesting over two years with a three-month cliff. Don't put promotional content or affiliate links on your own channels for products you don't actively use, advise, or hold real equity in.If you're a founder or investor:Separate partner programs from hiring. If you need channel distribution, build an explicit, transparent partner program. Don't route affiliate recruiting through a hiring funnel.Pay for advisory work like it's real work. Strategic advisory requires judgment and time. Compensate it with equity or a cash retainer, not a capped, contingent payout. How you treat candidates during hiring is visible to investors too. Using a hiring funnel to subsidize an unpaid sales team reads as an inability to build a real GTM engine, and that's a flag in diligence.Building Growth That Doesn't Need ThisReal growth leverage comes from transparent systems, real data integration, and incentives that are actually aligned. A funnel that runs on candidate misdirection might produce a few warm intros, but it burns trust with the exact people a company will need again later, and it usually signals that the underlying product-market fit isn't there yet.Treat hiring with the same integrity you'd want applied to your own customer acquisition. If the role is a job, pay for it like one.What is the "Fake Executive Funnel"?It's a hiring pattern where a company posts a salaried executive role, uses the interview process to extract the candidate's GTM strategy and account targets, then pivots the offer to an unpaid, commission-only advisory agreement instead of a real job.Did you sign the agreement?No. The terms (unpaid, capped, with a long payment lag and no real pipeline visibility) weren't close to a fair trade for the work being asked. I passed on the advisory version and kept looking.Is a revenue-share advisory agreement illegal?Not inherently. Advisory and referral agreements are common and can be legitimate. The problem is the bait-and-switch: recruiting for a salaried role, extracting proprietary strategy during the process, then converting to a commission-only deal without disclosing that intent upfront.What's a standard equity range for a startup advisor?The widely used benchmark is the Founder Institute FAST Agreement: roughly 0.25% to 1.0% equity, vesting over two years with a three-month cliff, for a defined scope of advisory work.How is this different from a normal affiliate or partner program?A real partner program is disclosed as one from the start; both sides know they're negotiating a referral deal, not a job. This pattern disguises that same arrangement as executive recruiting to get free strategic work during the interview process.What should I ask if a job offer suddenly turns into an advisory role?Ask for the guaranteed base compensation or standard equity structure for the original scope of work. If there isn't one, and the "advisory" terms include revenue share, a long payment lag, or discretionary lead rejection, treat it as a commission-only sales contract, not a job.

item.title: 7 Questions for Assessing Cyber Resilience Act Codebase Readiness
item.author: Sonar
item.content:encoded: September is here, and for different people it means different things—kids begin their school years, teens are off to university, and manufacturers of products with digital elements that sell them in the European Union are getting ready for mandatory reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting their products.The European Commission gave businesses time to prepare, but the deadline can still sneak up on you, particularly for organizations that are not used to regulated product security. If you’re feeling unprepared, the best place to start is to establish where you are now and turn your gaps into a focused action plan.Before we jump into what to do, let’s examine what’s about to happen. In practical terms, from 11 September 2026, manufacturers will be required to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting the security of products with digital elements. Three components matter here: who has to report, where the report goes and what triggers the obligation. A manufacturer of products with digital elements that are in scope of CRA must notify regulators about any actively exploited vulnerability contained in its product with digital elements that it becomes aware of. The notification should be submitted through the Single Reporting Platform and made available simultaneously to the Computer Security Incident Response Team (CSIRT) designated as coordinator and to ENISA.An actively exploited vulnerability is defined as “a vulnerability for which there is reliable evidence that a malicious actor has exploited it in a system without permission of the system owner.” It's important to remember that even though it's an organization's call to action, the regulator will also be making their own call during audits/assessments to figure out if appropriate action was taken. also have a specific framing in the regulation. An incident having an impact on the security of a product with digital elements is considered severe where:(a) it negatively affects or is capable of negatively affecting the ability of a product with digital elements to protect the availability, authenticity, integrity or confidentiality of sensitive or important data or functions; or(b) it has led or is capable of leading to the introduction or execution of malicious code in a product with digital elements or in the network and information systems of a user of the product with digital elements.Both have to be reported through a Single Reporting Platform during the first 24 hours after an organization has become aware of the occurrence of a security event.Now, let's look at how to assess where you stand today—whether you're ready, what extra steps you need, and what carries you forward to 2027.Assessing your codebase’s CRA readinessTo assess your codebase’s CRA readiness, use the following seven questions:Are secure defaults encoded in the codebase, with security controls enabled and unnecessary capabilities disabled?Are changes to security-critical code and configuration identified, reviewed and tested?Can every release be traced to its exact source, build inputs and dependencies?Must every code change pass the applicable security checks before it can merge?Can the build or release be blocked when serious security findings remain?Do automated tests exercise security-critical code against misuse and hostile input?Do release tests verify the security behavior implemented by the code?For each question, assess the current control as: absent or unknown. partial, inconsistent or manually dependent. defined, evidenced and consistently applied. automated where appropriate and able to prevent progression.An answer below Standard indicates that the control is not yet reliably established.The reporting relevance describes how the control supports the Article 14 obligations applying from 11 September 2026, it does not mean that Article 14 expressly requires that particular codebase control.Question: Are secure defaults encoded in the codebase, with security controls enabled and unnecessary capabilities disabled?If below Standard: The codebase does not reliably establish a secure initial state. Security may depend on users, operators or deployment teams changing permissions, disabling features or correcting insecure settings.Reporting relevance: Secure defaults reduce the likelihood that an unsafe initial configuration results in an actively exploited vulnerability or severe incident that must be reported.Broad CRA fit: Annex I, Part I, point 2(b) requires products to be made available with a secure-by-default configuration, subject to limited exceptions.2. Security-sensitive changesQuestion: Are changes to security-critical code and configuration identified, reviewed and tested?If below Standard: Security-sensitive changes may enter the codebase without being recognized or receiving the additional review and testing they require.Reporting relevance: Identifying security-sensitive changes makes it easier to investigate how a vulnerability or incident was introduced, determine the affected versions and explain the corrective action taken.Broad CRA fit: Supports the effective and regular security testing and review required by Annex I, Part II, point 3. Question: Can every release be traced to its exact source, build inputs and dependencies?If below Standard: The organization may be unable to establish exactly what code and third-party components are present in a release, making vulnerability assessment, remediation and component inventory less reliable.Reporting relevance: Release traceability helps identify affected versions and components, assess the impact of a vulnerability and determine the appropriate corrective or mitigating measure.Broad CRA fit: Annex I, Part II, point 1 requires manufacturers to identify and document product components and vulnerabilities, including through an SBOM covering at least top-level dependencies. Exact build traceability goes beyond the minimum wording but supports an accurate inventory for each release.4. Pre-merge security checksQuestion: Must every code change pass the applicable security checks before it can merge?If below Standard: Security checks are absent, inconsistent or dependent on individual teams, allowing changes to enter the main codebase without the required security assessment.Reporting relevance: Pre-merge checks help find weaknesses before they reach a released product and potentially become actively exploited. They support prevention rather than the reporting process itself.Broad CRA fit: Supports regular security testing and review under Annex I, Part II, point 3 and helps prevent releases containing known exploitable vulnerabilities under Annex I, Part I, point 2(a). Question: Can the build or release be blocked when serious security findings remain?If below Standard: Security findings may inform release decisions, but they do not reliably prevent code with unresolved serious weaknesses from being shipped.Reporting relevance: Blocking a release with unresolved serious findings reduces the likelihood that a known weakness enters the market and later becomes actively exploited or contributes to a severe incident.Broad CRA fit: This supports Annex I, Part I, point 2(a), concerning known exploitable vulnerabilities, and Annex I, Part II, point 2, concerning the remediation of vulnerabilities without delay. Blocking thresholds and controlled exceptions should reflect the product’s cybersecurity risk assessment.6. Testing against misuseQuestion: Do automated tests exercise security-critical code against misuse and hostile input?If below Standard: Testing mainly covers expected behaviour and may not reveal how security-critical code responds to malformed input, abuse cases or deliberate attempts to bypass controls.Reporting relevance: Security testing can expose vulnerabilities before active exploitation and help establish their severity, impact and the effectiveness of a proposed fix.Broad CRA fit: This supports the effective and regular testing required by Annex I, Part II, point 3 and helps verify relevant Annex I, Part I properties, including access control, data protection, attack-surface reduction and exploit mitigation.7. Runtime security behaviourQuestion: Do release tests verify the security behaviour implemented by the code?If below Standard: The release process does not reliably demonstrate that security-critical behaviour—such as update integrity, rollback protection, isolation, secure deletion or resilience under stress—works as intended at runtime.Reporting relevance: Runtime testing helps determine whether an incident meets the severity threshold, assess its effect on the product and verify that corrective or mitigating measures work as intended.Broad CRA fit: Supports Annex I requirements relating to secure updates, confidentiality, integrity, availability, resilience, and security-event monitoring, together with the effective and regular testing requirement in Annex I, Part II, point 3. Once you understand the current status of your codebase, prioritize your key actions. Address the important gaps before they turn into compliance problems, weighted by how much of your product's risk sits behind each control. A missing secure default on an internet-facing product moves ahead of a missing pre-merge check on an internal tool. Revisit the questionnaire on a fixed cadence so that Standard today does not quietly slip back to Ad hoc by next audit.How can Sonar help manufacturers prepare for the Cyber Resilience Act?Preparing for CRA based on the questionnaire above may sound overwhelming, particularly if the controls are spread across multiple tools or executed manually. Given the volume of code that needs to be assessed (and the number of potential issues that may need to be addressed) a predominantly manual approach is unlikely sustainable. Adoption creates another challenge: when compliance-related work requires a separate workflow or introduces significant friction, it is less likely to be applied consistently, creating avoidable gaps. Because a missed control can allow a vulnerability to reach a released product, security checks should be placed inside the workflows already used by software developers and AI coding agents. SonarQube supports this model by bringing analysis, review and enforcement into IDE/agentic generation loop, pull request and CI/CD workflows, while producing evidence that codebase security controls are operating consistently. For CRA codebase readiness, that support breaks down as follows:Consistent security baseline: Centrally managed quality profiles define which reliability and security rules apply.Earlier feedback and constraints for developers and coding agents: Connected analysis brings centrally managed rules into the IDE, while Sonar Vortex guides and verifies AI-generated changes against the organization’s standards inside the agentic coding loop, allowing issues to be identified before code is committed or submitted for review.Software composition analysis identifies direct and transitive dependencies and known dependency risks. CycloneDX or SPDX SBOMs provide component inventories, and separate VEX information records assessed vulnerability status.Vulnerability identification and remediation: Static analysis, secrets detection and infrastructure-as-code analysis identify weaknesses in code and configuration, while Hunter Agent extends detection to business-logic, access-control and authentication flaws. Gitar supports remediation in new code, and SonarQube Remediation Agent addresses the existing backlog. Quality gates and pull request decoration provide a pass-or-fail signal based on defined conditions for code, including security findings and dependency risks, making sure that no sub-par code is able to pass to production. Test coverage data and supported external analysis results provide additional evidence of regular testing and review.Evidence and reporting support: Analysis history, quality gate results, issue status and remediation records help evidence operating controls and identify affected code, dependencies and corrective measures.Together, these capabilities support accelerated codebase-side readiness for the 11 September 2026 reporting deadline by improving issue discovery, affected version analysis and remediation evidence, while establishing the preventive controls needed for broader CRA readiness ahead of 11 December 2027.But how do we know that it works for code created by AI agents?Easy: developer workflow powered by Sonar has been tested repeatedly at enterprise scale over our 16+ year history, with agentic acceleration capabilities being highly regarded by major market players in 2026. At Cisco, an internal agent uses SonarQube issue context to plan fixes and create pull requests, helping resolve 27,000 issues in three months. A global financial institution requires AI-assisted teams to use its SonarQube pipeline across approximately 20,000 engineers and 8,500 projects. Freshworks applies quality gates across more than 2,000 repositories as AI adoption grows, while Xero applies the same standards to human- and AI-generated code across 3,500 repositories. At IMSA, the same model supports mandatory checks across more than 2,000 projects. Across these organizations, verification is not slowing delivery; it is helping human- and AI-generated code scale with greater control.How to get ready for Cyber Resilience Act The reporting deadline lands on 11 September 2026, and the broader CRA obligations follow on 11 December 2027. Both are close enough that the tooling you pick now is the tooling you will still be relying on then. SonarQube is built for that stretch: consistent baselines inside the workflows your software developers and AI agents already use, and an evidence trail that makes readiness demonstrable at audit.Talk to our team about getting CRA-ready—and give procurement enough runway that it does not become the delay factor you did not plan for.

item.title: Climate 'Feedback Loops' Could Worsen Global Warming By 30%, Study Finds
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Rising global temperatures caused by the burning of fossil fuels are transforming the world's forests, wetlands and tundra to the point they are releasing emissions that could further worsen global heating by as much as 30%, a new study has found. As the world heats up, permafrost in the high latitudes is thawing, fiercer wildfires are burning in drying forests and wetlands and lakes are warming. All of these changes are themselves causing the release of planet-heating methane and carbon dioxide locked in trees and soils, therefore worsening the climate crisis, the paper states.
While scientists have long known of these "feedback loops" that amplify the impact of direct pollution from burning coal, oil and gas, the emissions from natural sources are largely unaccounted for in climate projections. This additional heating is however significant, researchers found, with emissions from natural sources set to amplify global heating by 20% to 30% by the end of this century. This would add an estimated 0.2C to 0.4C to the global average temperature by this time, depending on the overall action taken by countries to combat the climate crisis.
[...] This latest paper makes clear that action by countries to cut fossil fuel pollution will still lessen the amount of additional emissions that come from landscapes. Under the most optimistic climate scenario where emissions are cut quickly, natural sources will add 0.2C of warming, the paper found. Under a worse case higher emissions scenario, 0.4C will likely be added. Current policies put in place by governments are likely to see the global temperature rise to 2.6C above pre-industrial times, according to Climate Action Tracker. This will likely cause severe disruption and hardship to billions of people through sea level rise, crop losses and other consequences. "This hidden multiplier is missing from the models guiding climate policy, so those models are likely underestimating how much warming is coming -- and overestimating how much carbon we can still afford to emit," said Sam Abernethy, a scientist at Spark Climate Solutions who led the research, published in Environmental Research Letters.
The disruption of the worldâ(TM)s carbon cycles is now being seen in "real time," said Rob Jackson, a Stanford University scientist and study co-author. "The results are a wake-up call, and itâ(TM)s imperative that they be included in the next generation of climate policies," he added. "Failure to do so will make meeting the worldâ(TM)s climate goals less and less likely."

item.title: What 46,000 Production Queries Taught Us About LLM-Generated SQL
item.author: Christian Richter
item.content:encoded:
We run a financial data server that sits on top of a 31-million-row DuckDB database. Users connect an LLM (usually Claude), ask questions in plain English, and the model generates SQL against our schema.Over six months we logged every query: the user's natural language prompt, the SQL the LLM produced, whether it succeeded, how long it took, and how many rows came back. 46k queries total.The database covers 64 years of US stock market data across 12 tables: daily prices and volume (31M rows), quarterly and yearly financials, daily valuations, 56 technical indicators, SEC filing metadata, insider transactions, analyst estimates, and company reference data. About 9,971 securities (stocks and ETFs) on NYSE and NASDAQ.Users connect to it via MCP (Model Context Protocol), the open standard that lets LLMs call external tools. When a user asks "show me US stocks with 3 consecutive quarters of revenue growth and expanding margins," the LLM reads our schema, reads a query pattern library, generates SQL, and executes it. The full round trip, prompt to result table, takes 2-3 seconds on average.The secret weapon: a 674-line pattern libraryWe did not fine-tune a model. We did not build a RAG pipeline over example queries. We wrote a 674-line markdown document containing 23 SQL patterns and gave it to the LLM as context before every query.Each pattern solves a specific problem that trips up LLMs on large time-series databases. The most important one:-- Pattern P1: Latest row per symbol (multi-symbol safe) WITH recent AS ( SELECT symbol, date, close, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY date DESC) AS rn FROM shibui.stock_quotes WHERE date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days' -- pre-filter first ) SELECT symbol, date, close FROM recent WHERE rn = 1 LIMIT 50 Three things happen in this pattern. The WHERE date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days' pre-filters before the window function runs, keeping the working set small. The idiom gets the latest row per symbol without ambiguity. The prevents runaway result sets.Without this pattern, an LLM will happily write SELECT * FROM stock_quotes ORDER BY date DESC and try to scan 31 million rows. With it, the same intent produces a query that finishes in milliseconds.The library covers 22 more patterns: return calculations, quarter-over-quarter growth with , multi-table screening joins, technical indicator lookups, sector benchmarks with , backtesting with calendar-period OHLC bars, and insider transaction aggregation.46% of queries use JOINs. 44% use CTEs. 40% use window functions. 30% touch two or more tables. The longest query is 22,828 characters. One query used 59 window functions. Another used 19 JOINs.
