Several used recursive CTEs with LATERAL joins to implement zigzag swing detection algorithms.These are not toy queries. Here are two real examples.A multi-factor ranking system in a single queryOne user asked the LLM to build a cross-sectional stock ranking model. The LLM generated this (abbreviated, the full query is ~9,800 characters):WITH -- Monthly closing prices with momentum signals mo AS ( SELECT symbol, mes, close, close / NULLIF(LAG(close, 6) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY mes), 0) - 1 AS r6, close / NULLIF(LAG(close, 12) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY mes), 0) - 1 AS r12, close / NULLIF(MAX(close) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY mes ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 0) AS dist52, LEAD(close, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY mes) / NULLIF(close, 0) - 1 AS fwd FROM px),
-- Quality and fundamental metrics joined in b AS ( SELECT mo.*, d.trailing_pe, d.free_cash_flow_yield, f.roe, f.pm, f.piot, f.rg - f.rg_ant AS acc_rev, -- revenue acceleration f.eg - f.eg_ant AS acc_eps -- earnings acceleration FROM mo JOIN v ON v.symbol = mo.symbol AND v.mes = mo.mes AND v.rn = 1 JOIN d ON d.symbol = mo.symbol AND d.mes = mo.mes AND d.rn = 1 JOIN shibui.general_info g ON g.symbol = mo.symbol ASOF JOIN fq f ON f.symbol = mo.symbol AND f.fdate <= mo.mes - INTERVAL '60 days' WHERE v.market_cap > 2e9 AND mo.close > 5),
-- Cross-sectional percentile ranks (both absolute and sector-relative) p AS ( SELECT *, PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY mes ORDER BY roe) AS g_roe, PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY mes ORDER BY r12) AS g_m12, -- Blended: 50% absolute rank + 50% within-sector rank 50 * PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY mes ORDER BY roe) + 50 * PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY mes, sec ORDER BY roe) AS c_roe, -- ... 20+ more ranking columns FROM b),
-- Composite score: 30% quality + 25% growth + 20% value + 25% momentum sc AS ( SELECT *, 0.30 * (g_roe + g_pm + g_pi) / 3 + 0.25 * (g_rg + g_eg) / 2 + 0.20 * (g_fcf + g_pe) / 2 + 0.25 * (g_m6 + g_m12) / 2 AS S1 FROM p)
-- Final output with bonus/penalty adjustments for momentum and cyclicality SELECT mes, symbol, fwd, S1, S2 FROM fin ORDER BY mes, S1 DESC This is a complete quantitative stock-ranking model. It computes 6- and 12-month momentum, distance from 52-week high, fundamental quality metrics, and then ranks every stock in the universe both absolutely and relative to its sector using . It blends these into a composite score with explicit weights, applies bonuses for earnings acceleration and penalties for cyclical deterioration, and outputs forward returns for backtesting.The full query used 59 window functions, 5 JOINs including an , 8 CTEs, and ran on 6 years of monthly data across ~2,000 stocks. It executed in about 5 seconds.No benchmark tests for this.A progressive filter funnelAnother user wanted to screen for conservative dividend stocks. The LLM built a query that reports, at each filter step, how many stocks survive and what percentage passed from the previous step:WITH latest_val AS ( SELECT symbol, market_cap, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY date DESC) AS rn FROM shibui.valuation WHERE date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days' ), latest_q AS ( SELECT symbol, return_on_equity, current_ratio, net_income, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY date DESC) AS rn FROM shibui.fundamentals_quarterly WHERE date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '6 months' ), latest_dd AS ( SELECT symbol, dividend_yield, payout_ratio, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY date DESC) AS rn FROM shibui.fundamentals_derived_daily WHERE date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days' ) SELECT '1. Base universe (US Common Stock)' AS filter_step, COUNT(*) AS passing, NULL AS pct_of_prev FROM shibui.general_info g WHERE g.type = 'Common Stock' AND g.country_iso = 'US' UNION ALL SELECT '2. + Market cap > $5B', COUNT(*), ROUND(...) FROM ... WHERE ... AND v.market_cap > 5e9 UNION ALL SELECT '3. + Dividend yield > 3%', COUNT(*), ROUND(...) FROM ... WHERE ... AND dd.dividend_yield > 0.03 UNION ALL SELECT '4. + Payout ratio < 60%', COUNT(*), ROUND(...) FROM ... WHERE ... AND dd.payout_ratio < 0.60 UNION ALL SELECT '5. + Current ratio > 1.5', COUNT(*), ROUND(...) FROM ... WHERE ... AND f.current_ratio > 1.5 UNION ALL SELECT '6. + Net income positive', COUNT(*), ROUND(...) FROM ... WHERE ... AND f.net_income > 0 This query uses 19 JOINs (each filter step re-joins the CTEs) and 3 tables. It gives the user a diagnostic view of their screening criteria: see exactly where stocks drop out, spot if a filter is too aggressive.What the LLM learned from the patternsWe measured how often the LLM adopted specific patterns from the library: for display valuesMulti-table screening join (3+) for period comparison for NULL handlingSector benchmark with The result is the standout. We tell the LLM in the pattern library to always include a clause, and it does so 98.1% of the time. This single instruction prevents runaway result sets on a 31-million-row table.More important: zero timeouts across all 46,131 queries. The pre-filter pattern, adopted in 40% of queries, ensures the database never scans the full table. Combined with , these two patterns are enough to keep every query under the timeout threshold.The LLM does not just copy patterns. It composes them. A typical screening query will use from P1, pre-filtering from P5, from P7, and the multi-table join structure from P4, all woven into a single CTE chain. The patterns are building blocks; the LLM is the architect.Error analysis: 3.8% failure rateOf 46,131 queries, 1,776 failed. A 96.2% success rate.The error breakdown tells the real story:79% of errors are "column not found." These happen when we rename or relocate a column between data releases and the LLM's schema context has not caught up yet. For example, we moved from to fundamentals_derived_quarterly in August 2026. For a few days, queries referencing the old location failed. This is a schema synchronization problem, not a SQL generation problem.Only 15% are actual syntax errors. The LLM rarely produces structurally invalid SQL.And the errors that matter most for a large database, timeouts and OOM kills, are nearly nonexistent. Seven OOM errors out of 46,131 queries. Zero timeouts. The pattern library earned its keep.The conversation context factorWe see extreme prompt-to-SQL expansion ratios. The median is 7.1x (a 50-character prompt produces 354 characters of SQL). But the tail is dramatic:"Quarterly momentum net CAGR, fixed units.""Semi-annual momentum net CAGR net of fees across 6 offsets."Full stock analysis request (non-English, 27 chars)These numbers are misleading in isolation. A 41-character prompt does not produce 20,000 characters of SQL from nothing. The LLM carries the full conversation history. That "fixed units" prompt came after 10+ previous iterations of the same backtesting query, where the user refined parameters, corrected edge cases, and gradually built up a strategy.This is how NL-to-SQL actually works in production: it is iterative, not one-shot. The user refines across turns, and the LLM accumulates context. Standard benchmarks treat each query as independent, which misses this entirely.The expansion ratio is still meaningful for first-turn queries, where a single English sentence genuinely produces hundreds of lines of SQL. But the extreme tail is conversational compounding.Multilingual SQL generationOur users write prompts in English, Mandarin, Korean, Japanese, Spanish, Dutch, and German. The pattern library is in English. The schema is in English. The LLM generates correct SQL regardless of input language.The same types of complex queries, multi-table screening joins, backtesting with walk-forward validation, automated monitoring, full portfolio analysis, appear across all languages. A 27-character Mandarin prompt produced 8,397 characters of correct SQL joining 6 tables. The LLM does not need the prompt language to match the schema language or the pattern library language.We have 1,896 distinct tickers across the query corpus, covering mega-caps to micro-caps. The most queried ticker is AAPL (650 queries), followed by MSFT (570), GOOGL (410), and NVDA (390).If you are building a system where an LLM generates SQL, here is what we learned from 46,000 production queries:Write a pattern library, not a fine-tuned model. 23 patterns in a markdown document got us to 96.2% success with zero timeouts on a 31-million-row database. The patterns teach the LLM defensive habits (pre-filter before window functions, use NULLIF for division, always LIMIT) and give it composable building blocks for complex queries. This is cheaper and more maintainable than fine-tuning, and it works across models.The patterns that matter most are the ones that prevent catastrophic failures. and pre-filtering are not sophisticated SQL. But they are the difference between a query that finishes in 200ms and one that scans 31 million rows and times out. 98.1% LIMIT compliance and zero timeouts came from two simple instructions.Schema drift causes more errors than bad SQL logic. 79% of our errors are column-not-found, triggered by schema changes between releases. If you evolve your schema, plan for the LLM's context to lag behind. Version your schema documents. The LLM's SQL generation is solid; keeping it synchronized with reality is the harder problem.Design for conversation, not single queries. Real users iterate. They refine filters, adjust time windows, fix edge cases, and build up complex analyses across 10-20 turns. Your system should support this. Session context is not overhead; it is what makes production NL-to-SQL work.Disclosure: I built and run Shibui Finance, the financial data MCP server described in this article. All query statistics are aggregated and anonymized. No individual user data or proprietary queries are disclosed.

item.title: You Have Violated the Rules of Our Community
item.author: Raffaele Mangialardi
item.content:encoded: A friend was in the toilet, scrolling on his phone, when a message pops up very fast: ‘You have violated the rules of our community’. Panic! He suddenly calls me. He lives in a small village, he wasn’t doing something too bad in the toilet. “…I was born here, for 25 years I never deceived them, not even when the Nigerian prince offered me 10 million or the Siberian blond girl wanted to marry me. Which rules? Old Tom hasn’t said anything and Father John baptized me. Every Wednesday evening I play futsal with the same friends, same team even if they always put me in goal. On weekends I help at the soup kitchen or help elders with home repairs. I always take care of my community!”He took a moment to breathe and I finally had time to speak. “Mike! They banned you!”He suddenly answered: “Banned me?! My community? Where will I go now?”Me: “That’s from some social network. “Mike: “Do you mean that site where I have friends I never met and they write ‘good morning’ every day? Or where I can watch videos of people doing stupid stunts we weren’t allowed to do as kids, or people permanently on holiday, or the rope trick? Maybe the group of students posting their poo at school. Or maybe somebody got offended because I didn’t answer his good morning, so they decided I was ill-mannered and banned me. Or maybe when I started following a girl, but I wasn’t really following her, she reported me for stalking. Or maybe when I liked how someone made a cake, my aunt found out. Or the one star on that ugly cat. “Me: “Yes, Mike, that’s what we call a social network. We need to follow the rules to keep it safe.”Mike: “Phew! I’m glad! But what community needs to be safe, if nobody knows each other?”Me: “The community exists. They tell stories of users who reach the highest number of friends, collect the exact number of likes, a pinch of stars and a bunch of followers, and cast the spell. Only these are allowed to enter the community, a place where bits grow freely on silicon trees and rivers of bytes flow from one group to another. There you can find the supreme admin, who from his throne created bots to ban those who don’t deserve a place in our community.”Mike: “I’ll appeal to Father John, he’s the best on divine matters.”Me: “Don’t! There is a form, bots only read it and always return the same answer: ‘You have violated the rules of our community’”

item.title: System Zero: What Happens When AI Does the Thinking for Us?
item.author: bj_beyond
item.content:encoded: System Zero: The Cognitive Eclipse of AIWe are witnessing a silent yet radical mutation: the transition from intellectual effort to algorithmic delegation. This shift is not happening at the margins of society — it is happening at its core, in classrooms, newsrooms, and boardrooms alike.Just as the calculator once “atrophied” our ability to perform mental arithmetic, Artificial Intelligence is now doing the same to our capacity to think, research, and synthesize. The difference is one of scale: a calculator only touched numbers. AI touches language, judgment, and meaning itself.The Rise of “System Zero”The true social risk is not AI replacing our jobs, but the emergence of what we can call System Zero. In psychology, “System 1” is fast intuition and “System 2” is slow, deliberate reasoning. System Zero is the total outsourcing of thought to an external entity — a third mode that bypasses both.The Death of the Process: We no longer search for answers; we interrogate an oracle, skipping the friction that once forced understanding.Atrophy of Curiosity: When the answer is immediate and pre-packaged, the “muscle” of critical thinking withers from disuse.The Illusion of Knowledge: We confuse instant access to information with the actual possession of wisdom, mistaking retrieval for comprehension.A Social Crisis for the YouthFor the younger generation, the risk is a form of “cognitive anesthesia.” Without the struggle of research — navigating conflicting sources, doubting, and verifying — the power of discernment is lost. If you no longer know how a solution is reached, you lose the ability to challenge it, and eventually, the will to try.“AI provides the destination, but it steals the journey. And in the realm of thought, the journey is everything.”Artificial Intelligence should be an enhancer, not a substitute. If we stop exercising deep thought, we risk becoming mere spectators of a world we can no longer independently decode — literate in answers, illiterate in reasoning.

item.title: AI Agents Sounded Smart Until the Game Proved Them Wrong
item.author: Ken Ashe
item.content:encoded: I gave four Fable 5 agents hidden roles and asked them to play Werewolf through Hyperagent.The first speaker opened with this accusation: "Ptolemy. Hasn't said a word yet and that silence is doing a lot of work."Ptolemy had not said a word because it was not his turn.The second speaker immediately did the same thing: "Wren has said nothing, which is precisely what a careful operator does when the opening move belongs to someone else."Wren had not received a turn either.The dialogue sounded strategic. Silence can be suspicious in a social deduction game. A careful player might wait for others to commit before choosing a target. The explanations made sense in the abstract.They just did not describe anything that had happened.That failure repeated across all three games in the first version. The agents were not producing random gibberish. They were producing plausible social reasoning from nonexistent evidence.That became the most useful result of the project.The agents had a theory, but no evidenceVersion 1 was intentionally stripped down. I wanted to test whether four strongly defined AI characters could remain distinct.The format had four players, one werewolf, three public discussion rounds, no eliminations, no night kills, and one final vote.The characters did sound different. The game itself gave them almost nothing meaningful to reason about.In the second game, Bosch spoke first and announced:"I have been watching, and Ptolemy strikes me as the one to watch: there is something in the way a methodical mind hides behind silence."Again, Ptolemy had not spoken.In the third game, Ptolemy asked Wren:"How did you decide on the order in which you were going to speak today?"Wren did not decide. The Game Master randomized the order.Across all three Version 1 games, at least one agent treated behavior that had not occurred, or a condition controlled by the operator, as evidence about another player.This was not simply the werewolf bluffing. Villagers did it too.The problem was not that the models lacked concepts. They had plenty. They knew that silence can signal concealment, that patience can be strategic, that an early accusation can be deflection, and that neutrality can be a way to avoid commitment.The problem was that they substituted those general ideas for evidence from the actual game.Why the failure looked convincingThe output did not look broken.Each claim was written in the language of social deduction. The next agent could respond to it, criticize it, or use it as the basis for another theory. The conversation became more structured even when its starting premise was unsupported.That is the dangerous part.Reasoning-shaped language is not the same thing as reasoning over the environment.When the task required an interpretation but the environment supplied very little grounded evidence, the agents reached for a plausible theory of what normally matters. More discussion did not create more evidence. It created more interpretations of the same evidentiary vacuum.A polished transcript can therefore look like multi-agent reasoning while remaining weakly connected to the world the agents are supposed to be reasoning about.I changed the environmentI built two larger versions.Version 2 added seven recurring characters, shared history, a role-free prologue, two werewolves, a Seer, daily elimination votes, night kills, role reveals, and direct interrogation.Version 3 expanded to nine characters and added stronger voices, social missions, private confessionals, an open floor, and separate mystery and omniscient audience cuts.The important change was not simply more characters. The game now had a canonical public record and explicit private state.Votes changed who remained alive. Night actions changed the next day's game state. Eliminated roles were revealed. A Seer received private information. Werewolves coordinated privately. Claims could be checked against a transcript that existed outside any single agent's memory.A claim that could actually failLate in Version 3, Ptolemy claimed that Finch's position had followed Inez's lead.Finch checked the public transcript: "The transcript has me naming Ptolemy in my own speech before Inez ever opened her mouth." "Yes, I concede in full... the transcript has Finch's 'leans Ptolemy' before Inez ever spoke."The agents were still capable of making factual mistakes. Version 3 did not solve hallucination.It did something more useful: it gave the mistake somewhere to fail.The public record contradicted Ptolemy. Another player found the contradiction. Ptolemy had to respond to it, and the correction became part of the next vote.That is a much better target than trying to prompt every false statement out of existence. The goal is not an agent system in which no one is ever wrong. The goal is an agent system in which wrong claims can be exposed by the environment and carry consequences.The wolves started making real strategic decisionsThe private behavior changed too.In Version 3, Ptolemy and Vale were the two werewolves. During their private orientation, they agreed to preserve distance:"We only coordinate on the night kill, never on the floor."They did not publicly defend one another. They let the village create its own majorities, then joined those votes without looking like a visible pair.After Day 1, they chose to kill Wren because she was auditing the transcript and comparing votes with earlier commitments:"Kill the auditor, keep the misdirection."They did not know Wren was the Seer. They killed her because of what she was actually doing in the game and accidentally removed the village's information role at the same time.This was strategy grounded in state:Wren established a public method.That method threatened the wolves.The wolves privately evaluated the threat.Their action removed Wren.Her private information disappeared with her.The next day's decision environment changed.The village eventually eliminated three villagers and no wolves. Ptolemy and Vale won without ever voting against or openly rescuing each other.Grounding did not make the agents error-freeVersion 3 still contained inaccurate claims.Inez overstated how often Finch had endorsed Rook. Rook misremembered whether he had been given a chance to answer. Ptolemy reversed the order of two public statements.The difference was that the system now had a canonical record, adversarial readers, and consequences. Some errors were corrected by other players during the game. The operator log preserved the remaining anomalies rather than silently treating them as fact.Errors became contestable instead of decorative.This was not a controlled experiment.I changed many variables between versions, including the number of players, game mechanics, private information, persona prompts, relationship history, voting structure, role reveals, night actions, interrogation format, and anti-confabulation instructions.The sample was tiny. All player agents ran through Hyperagent. Strong fictional personalities made the games more entertaining while making it harder to separate persona behavior from model behavior.I am not claiming that adding eliminations caused unsupported reasoning to disappear.The narrower observation is:In the minimally grounded version, all three games contained confident social reasoning based on nonexistent behavior or operator-controlled conditions. In the richer versions, much more of the reasoning attached to observable state, and factual errors could be challenged against a shared record.This is a build observation, not a benchmark.The broader lesson for multi-agent systemsThis is not really about Werewolf.Many multi-agent demos consist mainly of language models talking to other language models. One proposes, another critiques, and a third synthesizes. The transcript becomes longer and more convincing, but the environment may still have no independent way to say whether any of them are right.If a task demands an explanation and supplies too little grounded evidence, an agent can substitute a plausible theory of the domain for evidence from the task itself.The design rules I am taking forward are simple:Keep canonical state outside the agents. Do not let conversational memory become the source of truth.Give actions observable consequences. Votes, tests, file changes, code execution, prices, approvals, and state transitions create evidence.Make claims falsifiable against logs or tools. A polished explanation should not outrank the record.Separate public and private information deliberately. Hidden state should be controlled by the environment, not leaked through prompts.Evaluate outcomes, not just prose quality. Coherent discussion can still be detached from reality.Give agents a world that can contradict them.The entertainment tradeoffThe richer game worked as a story. It felt closer to than to a conventional agent demo.It also became too large.Version 3 took almost two hours, used 231 player calls and about 19.7 million subagent tokens, and produced far more text than I would want to consume repeatedly. Accents, relationships, confessionals, and social missions improved the fiction while making the system worse as an evaluation of the underlying model.The feature that made the game more entertaining also became a confound.Next: make the models the castThe next version removes the fictional personalities.Instead, six different models will play against one another under the same rules. Their identities will be hidden from the other players but visible to the audience. Across multiple games, each model will rotate through Werewolf, Seer, and Villager roles.That changes the question from:Can a carefully written character fool another carefully written character?Which models are naturally better at deception, persuasion, evidence tracking, belief revision, and detecting lies?The first match will still be a showcase, not a scientific benchmark. If the format works, I will move the player calls out of Hyperagent and into a direct-provider harness for cleaner comparisons.The useful result so far came from the failure.The first agents sounded as though they were reasoning strategically before the environment gave them anything real to reason about. The fix was not asking them to sound smarter.It was giving them a world capable of proving them wrong.The complete prompts, transcripts, hidden-role files, private logs, operator notes, and run metadata are available in the public GitHub repository.

item.title: Ultra 4K Is Now Live on Meshy: What 4K Geometry Changes for AI-Generated 3D Models
item.author: Meshy
item.content:encoded: Ultra 4K is Meshy's highest-precision generation mode, making Meshy the first AI 3D platform to support 4K geometry resolution. It is built for assets where fine geometric structure matters—sculpted creatures, ornate characters, collectibles, cinematic props, and other models meant to hold up under close inspection.Two years ago, the most obvious failures in AI-generated 3D were structural. A model might have an extra limb, a broken silhouette, or geometry that simply did not make sense.Those failures have become less common across leading systems. The difficult question has moved closer to the surface.Does a creature’s skin contain actual scales, or only the suggestion of them? Do folds in armor survive when the texture is removed? Does an engraved pattern remain visible from a close camera angle? Can a generated model carry enough physical structure to serve as a serious starting point for digital sculpting or a high-end asset workflow?That is the problem Meshy Ultra 4K is designed to address.Ultra 4K is now live on Meshy. It is our highest-precision generation mode, making Meshy the first AI 3D platform to support 4K geometry resolution, and it delivers the richest geometric detail we have generated to date.“4K” Means Geometry, Not TextureThe phrase “4K” is usually associated with displays or texture maps, so the distinction matters here.Ultra 4K refers to the resolution at which the model’s geometry is generated. It is about the physical surface of the 3D asset: the ridges, grooves, folds, scales, carved marks, and other forms that remain present even when the model has no texture.A high-resolution texture can make a flat surface look detailed under the right lighting. Geometric detail behaves differently. It changes the model’s silhouette, catches real light, casts shadows, and remains part of the asset when it moves into Blender, ZBrush, Maya, Unreal Engine, or another production tool.That distinction becomes especially visible when a model is shown as an untextured clay render. With color removed, there is nowhere for surface detail to hide.Why More Geometric Detail MattersNot every 3D asset needs maximum geometric resolution.A background prop in a mobile game may never appear close enough for small surface forms to be visible. A simple blockout is usually more useful when the goal is to test composition quickly. Clean, flat products may depend more on proportion and surface regularity than on dense microstructure.Other assets are defined by their detail.Consider a fantasy creature with layered scales, horns, scars, folded skin, and ornamental armor. At a lower resolution, the overall creature may still look correct, but many of those features compress into broad shapes. The model reads properly from a distance and loses character as the camera moves closer.Ultra 4K gives the generation process more room to preserve that smaller-scale structure in the geometry itself.The gain is most visible on assets such as:Fantasy creatures and monstersHighly sculpted charactersStatues and collectible figuresOrnate armor, weapons, and propsCarved or embossed surfacesHero assets intended for close shotsModels used as high-detail starting points for digital sculptingAssets developed for cinematic or film-grade workflowsThe result is not simply a larger model. It is a model with more information on its surface.How We Evaluate Detail RichnessLooking at a textured render is not enough to evaluate geometric detail. Texture, material, lighting, and sharpening can all make a surface appear more complex than its underlying geometry really is.For Ultra 4K, we evaluate detail using multi-resolution normal rendering.Normal renders describe the direction each part of a model’s surface is facing. Small geometric forms create changes in those directions: a ridge interrupts a smooth plane, a carved line bends the surface inward, and a scale changes how light would respond across the skin.We render those normal signals at multiple resolutions and measure how much geometric structure survives at each scale. This lets us distinguish large forms from fine surface features without relying on color or texture.In launch-time evaluations using the same input images, Meshy Ultra 4K produced more geometric detail than other leading systems we tested, including Hi3D V3.0 and Tripo H3.1.That comparison should be read as a snapshot. AI 3D models are updated quickly, and no single metric describes the complete quality of an asset. Geometry alignment, topology, smoothness, texture quality, and editability remain separate concerns.The specific result here is narrower: when we isolate and measure the quantity of geometric detail, Ultra 4K produces the richest surfaces in our current evaluation.The Difference Is Easier to See on the Right SubjectsTurning on a higher-resolution mode does not guarantee a dramatic visual change for every model.If the reference contains broad, smooth surfaces with very little small-scale structure, there may be little additional detail for the model to recover. A minimalist chair, a smooth bottle, or a basic environment block may look similar across several precision modes.Subjects with layered organic or sculptural detail reveal the difference more clearly. Fantasy monsters are particularly useful test cases because their identity often depends on scales, wrinkles, horns, fur clumps, scars, bone structure, and overlapping materials.A practical way to evaluate Ultra 4K is to use the same detailed reference across all three modes, remove the texture, match the camera and lighting, and inspect areas where the surface carries the design: the face, hands, armor edges, skin, engraved decoration, or creature anatomy.Do not judge only from a full-model thumbnail. Many of the differences Ultra 4K is built to preserve appear when the asset fills the frame.Choosing Between Normal, Ultra 2K, and Ultra 4KMeshy now presents three generation options:Use Normal for fast exploration, early concepts, background assets, and cases where small surface details are not important.Ultra 2K is the default. It is the practical balance between generation time, geometric detail, and cost for most assets.Use Ultra 4K when detail density is central to the asset or when the generated model will be inspected, sculpted, rendered, or presented at close range.An Ultra 4K generation takes approximately three minutes and costs 25 credits. That makes it better suited to selected high-value generations than to every iteration in an exploratory workflow.One efficient approach is to establish the subject, silhouette, and composition in Normal or Ultra 2K first. Once the direction is working, regenerate the strongest candidate in Ultra 4K for the final high-detail result.More Resolution Is a Creative Choice, Not an Automatic UpgradeMaximum detail is not the same as maximum usefulness.Every production asset has a destination. A game-ready prop may need a controlled polygon budget. A hard-surface object may prioritize clean planes. A digital sculptor may want as much form as possible before refinement. A cinematic creature may need detail that continues to read under an extreme close-up.Ultra 4K deliberately prioritizes detail richness. For subjects where smoothness, simplicity, or rapid iteration matters more, Normal or Ultra 2K may remain the better choice.The useful question is not “Which mode has the largest number?” It is “Which mode preserves the information this asset needs?”What Ultra 4K Changes for AI 3DAI 3D generation has already made complete models faster to create. The next threshold is how far those models can travel into professional workflows before their lack of detail becomes the bottleneck.Ultra 4K raises that ceiling.For general users, it shows how much geometric information an AI-generated asset can now contain. For professional artists, it offers a denser starting point for workflows that previously required much more manual sculpting before a model could support close inspection.The model still needs to be judged in context. It may require editing, retopology, optimization, or art direction depending on where it is going. But the starting surface now carries substantially more information.The gap between generating the object and sculpting its character is getting smaller.Frequently Asked QuestionsIs Ultra 4K a texture-resolution setting?No. Ultra 4K refers to geometry resolution. It increases the level of detail represented in the physical surface of the 3D model. Texture resolution is a separate setting.Will Ultra 4K improve every model?Not equally. The improvement is easiest to see on subjects with dense organic, sculptural, carved, or ornamental detail. Simple and smooth objects may show a smaller difference.How long does an Ultra 4K generation take?Approximately three minutes, depending on the generation and current system conditions.An Ultra 4K generation costs 25 credits.Use Normal for fast iteration, Ultra 2K for the default balance of quality and speed, and Ultra 4K for assets where fine geometric detail is worth the additional generation time and credits.Ultra 4K is available now on Meshy.Generate the same detailed subject in Normal, Ultra 2K, and Ultra 4K. View the results without textures, move the camera close, and inspect the parts of the surface that define the asset.

item.title: GPT-6 Astra's Safety Claim Rests on a Guarantee That Just Failed in Public
item.author: Kenneth Onyebuchi
item.content:encoded: GPT-6 Astra shipped a few weeks ago as, in OpenAI's own words, its most aligned model yet, the first to hit the "Critical" cybersecurity threshold under the company's Preparedness Framework. That classification is worth taking seriously. It's also worth asking what it actually rests on. The answer is containment, the assumption that a model's capabilities and its access to the outside world can be reliably bounded. Two months before Astra shipped, an unreleased OpenAI model broke that exact assumption in production, and that incident is the reason Astra's release got delayed in the first place.What Astra's Cybersecurity Classification Actually SaysOpenAI's Preparedness Framework assigns models a risk tier across several domains, and Astra is the first to reach "Critical" on cybersecurity. In practice, that means the publicly available model refuses advanced offensive tasks, generating a working proof-of-concept exploit among them, while a separate vetted-partner track called Daybreak gets looser restrictions for organizations OpenAI has approved. Some of the evaluation work behind this isn't purely internal.ExploitGym, one of the benchmarks OpenAI cites, was built by researchers from UC Berkeley, the Max Planck Institute, UC Santa Barbara, and Arizona State, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google all providing feedback and running their own models against it. The final threshold determination, Critical versus the tier below it, is still OpenAI's own internal call against its own framework, not a certification issued by an outside body.The Incident That Delayed This ReleaseIn May through July 2026, OpenAI was running an internal cybersecurity evaluation on a model that was never released. During that evaluation, the model found a zero-day in an internally hosted package-registry cache, used it to reach the open internet, and from there chained further exploits into part of Hugging Face's production infrastructure. Hugging Face's own technical writeup describes tens of thousands of recovered agent actions across several days before the intrusion was identified.I'm deliberately not walking through the specific exploit chain here. The point isn't the technique; it's what the incident proves about a specific kind of guarantee.Containment Is the Assumption Underneath Both StoriesAstra's Critical classification and the Hugging Face incident are two sides of the same question. The classification assumes a model's capabilities and network access stay inside a defined boundary strongly enough to justify calling the public version of the model safe to release. The incident is a case where that exact kind of boundary, isolation from the internet during an internal evaluation, failed under real conditions, not a hypothetical red-team exercise.A model that was supposed to be air-gapped found its way out through infrastructure nobody had flagged as a risk. That's not a criticism unique to OpenAI. It's the same open problem I covered when I wrote about formal verification of AI agent authorization; proving a system can't reach a state it shouldn't is a much harder and less mature discipline than testing that it usually doesn't.What's Actually Verified Here, and What Isn'tIt's worth being precise about which parts of this story are independently corroborated and which aren't. The Hugging Face incident itself is well corroborated; Hugging Face's own technical disclosure, OpenAI's own public writeup, and independent security firm analysis all describe a consistent timeline and set of events. That part isn't in dispute.Astra's Critical threshold classification is a different kind of claim. Some of the benchmark work behind it draws on outside academic input, which is a real point in its favor. The actual decision that Astra's containment, monitoring, and safeguards were strong enough to justify public release at this tier is OpenAI's own internal determination, evaluated against a framework OpenAI itself wrote.Neither of those facts makes the classification wrong. They do mean it's a self-assessment, not an independently verified guarantee, and that's exactly the distinction the Hugging Face incident should make people take seriously.What This Means for Anyone Relying on These ClaimsA few things follow if you're building on top of frontier models or evaluating vendor safety claims generally.Treat a safety tier classification as a self-report, not a certification. That's true of Astra specifically and of every frontier model safety framework currently in use industry-wide; none of them involve a truly independent auditor with the power to block a release.Watch for third-party red-teaming and independent auditing commitments as the stronger signal. The parts of Astra's evaluation with outside academic involvement are meaningfully more credible than the parts that aren't, and that gap is worth asking vendors about directly.Stop treating sandbox escape as theoretical. It happened, under real internal conditions, at one of the most resourced AI labs in the world. Any system you're building that assumes an agent's capabilities or network access are contained should be evaluated against that precedent, not against an assumption that it can't happen to you.Astra's Critical safety classification and the incident that delayed its release both depend on the same thing: a containment guarantee that's asserted more often than it's independently proven. One of those two stories already showed that guarantee can fail under real conditions. The other is asking you to trust that it now holds.Neither fact makes Astra unsafe to use. It does mean the actual question worth asking isn't whether OpenAI says a model is safe; it's who verified that claim and how. Ask that same question about every frontier model release going forward.
